entities.name: Callippus of Cyzicus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Callippus of Cyzicus (c. 369–309 BCE) was a foundational Greek astronomer and mathematician whose innovative adjustments to Eudoxus's geocentric model of the cosmos significantly refined the understanding of planetary motions during the Hellenistic period. Active primarily in Athens and his native Cyzicus, Callippus is celebrated for his eponymous Callippic Cycle, a sophisticated calendaric system that improved upon the Metonic Cycle, demonstrating a profound grasp of both celestial mechanics and practical chronology. His work, which posited additional spheres to account for observed irregularities in planetary movements, represented a critical step in the ancient world's quest for a comprehensive and predictive astronomical model, directly influencing later thinkers like Aristotle.

Building upon the intricate system of homocentric spheres proposed by Eudoxus of Cnidus, Callippus introduced seven additional spheres, increasing the total from Eudoxus's 27 to 34, to more accurately represent the retrograde motions and varying brightness of the planets. Specifically, he added two spheres each for the Sun and Moon, and one each for Mercury, Venus, and Mars, thereby creating a more precise, albeit still geocentric, mechanism for celestial prediction. His most enduring contribution, however, was the Callippic Cycle, established around 330 BCE. This cycle, comprising four Metonic Cycles (76 years), equated 940 lunations to 27,759 days, correcting the slight overestimation of the Metonic Cycle by removing one day every 76 years, thus achieving a more accurate synchronization of solar and lunar years.
